## Summary

Adds an **opt-in wheel rotational degree of freedom** for `BOGEY` contacts. When a contact declares both new elements, its wheel spin rate is resolved together with the existing ground friction Lagrange multipliers in `FGAccelerations::CalculateFrictionForces`:

```xml
<contact type="BOGEY" name="LEFT_MAIN">
  <!-- existing elements unchanged -->
  <wheel_radius unit="M"> 0.22 </wheel_radius>
  <wheel_inertia unit="KG*M2"> 0.124 </wheel_inertia>
</contact>
```

Today `wheel-speed-fps` follows the contact-point velocity kinematically, so wheels never spin up and touchdown spin-up drag is not modelled. With the new DOF:

- the tire tread force acts on the tread slip (axle ground speed − radius × spin), bounded by `static_friction` × normal force;
- that force reaches the airframe **through the axle** (moment arm = axle, not contact point) while the wheel receives the opposite torque, so the spin-up momentum comes out of the aircraft instead of being double-counted;
- brakes and rolling resistance become a torque between the wheel and the airframe (a new multiplier with a pure moment Jacobian), bounded by the existing braking friction force × radius. A braked wheel therefore holds the same force as the current anti-skid model, and steady rolling drag is unchanged.

Wheels in ground contact at initialization or trim start rolling without slip. In the air they spin down at the same 13 ft/s² tread rate as `wheel-speed-fps`, faster with brakes. New properties: `gear/unit[i]/wheel-spin-rad_sec` and `gear/unit[i]/wheel-tread-slip-fps`.

## Why

This comes from [OSFS](https://0sfs.github.io/) ([source](https://github.com/0SFS/0SFS.github.io)), an open-source browser flight simulator that runs JSBSim through WebAssembly. We added touchdown feedback (wheel spin-up visuals, tire sound, and gamepad/phone haptics) and wanted the wheels to act on the aircraft, rather than stay a one-way visual model:
- spin-up drag at touchdown;
- braking applied through the wheel.

Gear friction is resolved inside `CalculateFrictionForces` without a wheel rotation state. An application-side tire model would therefore double-count JSBSim's rolling and brake friction, and JavaScript cannot join the same constraint solve. So the only correct place for the wheel DOF was inside that solve, which is what this PR adds.

## Implementation

- `LagrangeMultiplier` gains optional fields: an explicit `MomentJacobian` (for torques that are not `r × F`) and a pointer to a `WheelSpinDOF` with the multiplier's Jacobian entry on the wheel spin.
- `FGAccelerations::CalculateFrictionForces` assembles `J M⁻¹ Jᵀ` and the right-hand side with the generalized rows (linear, angular, wheel) **only when some multiplier uses them**. Otherwise the original code path runs unchanged, so existing aircraft are unaffected.
- `FGLGear` parses the elements, owns the spin state, registers the roll row with the axle moment and wheel coupling plus the new wheel-brake row, integrates the spin with the previous solve's acceleration (in step with `FGPropagate`), and documents the elements in the class reference.

## Testing

- New `tests/TestWheelSpin.py`, registered in `tests/CMakeLists.txt`, using a sandboxed copy of `c172p` with the elements added:
  - opt-in, and invalid values disabling only that contact;
  - touchdown from an approach: no spin before contact, tread slip gone within 12 steps, no overshoot of rolling speed, and the extra loss of forward momentum matching the wheels' angular momentum;
  - rollout and braking deceleration within 5% of the unmodified model;
  - a ground start with no slip;
  - airborne spin-down with and without brakes.
- It fails against the current master, and passes with this change.
- `ctest` on macOS arm64 (Apple clang, Python 3.14, Cython 3.3, CxxTest 4.4), built from master `d0d8bc6e`: every test passes with this change (78 including `TestWheelSpin`). The exception is `TestInputSocket`, which times out in `telnetlib3`'s connection on this machine and passed 1 of 6 repeated runs both with and without the change. At the commit the patch was written against (`1a2e114d`), the full suite passed 76/76 without and 77/77 with it.
- Unmodified aircraft keep identical behaviour. With and without this change, a native build ran all 61 scripts in `scripts/`, plus a per-step log of position, velocity, attitude and gear forces/moments (1.8 M rows). All data outputs were byte-identical (checked at `1a2e114d`; the diff applies unchanged to `d0d8bc6e`). A WebAssembly build of c172p touchdown/rollout/braking/taxi/cruise traces is also bit-identical.

The C172 radii and inertias in the test are estimates from Goodyear's aviation data book (6.00-6 main, 5.00-5 nose tires), not measured assemblies. They only need to be plausible for the test.

Use `Jinv` for the inverse of the inertia for consistency with the rest of the code:
```suggestion
  double Jinv = 0.0; ///< 1 / spin inertia about the axle [1/(slug*ft^2)]
```
Renamed `InvInertia` to `Jinv` in “Use explicit moment Jacobians for friction.”
You should remove `LeverArm` now that you have introduced the moment jacobian, it would simplify the code using it everywhere.

Removed “absolute” in “Report wheel spin relative to the airframe.” I used
“ground reference frame,” matching the rate supplied to the solve.
`FGPropagate::GetPQR()` documents that rate as ECEF-relative; a transported
NED frame would require another correction. The state and its reference are
unchanged; the public property is now relative to the airframe.
Once having removed `LeverArm`, you will no longer need the lambda function `moment`.

Removed `LeverArm` and `UseMomentJacobian` in “Use explicit moment Jacobians
for friction.” All rows now supply their moment Jacobian.

I rechecked all 61 shipped XML inputs on the final candidate. Base and
original PR data match byte-for-byte; the cleanup changes 60 of 102 files
across 31 of 57 successful simulations. Crosswind reaches Δu = 0.0540 ft/s
and Δgear Fx = 197 lbf; the moored ZLT reaches Δgear yaw moment = 20,929
lbf·ft. F-16 Δu reaches 71.6 ft/s after severe ground impacts. These are
not uniformly rounding-sized output differences. The final candidate matches
the isolated cleanup probe exactly, and the PR body now reports these limits
instead of claiming existing aircraft are unaffected.
And the `continue` keyword to avoid an `else` is debatable...

This code should be located in the new method `ConfigureWheelSpinRows`. With the current code, it is far from obvious that when a wheel is accounted for, then the friction coefficient is `staticFFactor * staticFCoeff`. The reason for that is that with the current code in the PR, I was expecting the friction coefficient of `ftRoll` to be updated in `ConfigureWheelSpinRows`.

These variable names are misleading because `roll` is actually the direction of the roll friction force (unit vector) and `axle` is not the axle direction but the axle **position** with respect to the CG. And since the code is historically using *lever arm* to designate this position, then do so here as well.

Do not export the so-called *absolute spin rate*. Instead export the wheel spin rate measured with respect to the body frame. The latter is the spin rate that the Flight Control System and the Anti Blocking System will have access to (using a phonic wheel) in the real world.

Also it is the spin rate relative to the aircraft that 3D modelers need to display the wheels since models are generally organized through a hierarchy of bodies, each one being positioned relative to its parent in the hierarchy.

There is no "absolute" in JSBSim. Instead tell that it is the spin rate measured with respect to the NED frame.
```suggestion
  double Rate = 0.0;       ///< spin rate about the axle measured in the NED frame [rad/s]
```

Thanks @Felipegalind0 for your contribution. This PR is quite complex and it took me some time to understand what it does and how. For everyone, including my future self, the idea is to make wheels independent bodies from the aircraft. At its very core, JSBSim assumes that the aircraft is a single body and that other bodies are only interacting with the aircraft through the forces and moments that they apply to it. This is typically the case for propellers where `FGPropeller` is inheriting from `FGForce` via the `FGThruster` class: https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/propulsion/FGPropeller.h#L169 https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/propulsion/FGThruster.h#L77 The class `FGPropeller` manages its own body (the propeller!): * The propeller rotation rate is updated using its inertia and the angular momentum $I\dot{\theta}=\sum_i M_i$: https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/propulsion/FGPropeller.cpp#L294 * Forces and moments are computed and applied to the aircraft: https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/propulsion/FGPropeller.cpp#L282 https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/propulsion/FGPropeller.cpp#L300 The idea of the PR is to apply the same logic to the wheels using `FGLGear`: they become independent bodies with their own degree of freedom (DOF) and they apply a force and a moment to the aircraft. Above are free body diagrams of the wheel: the friction force $F_{\text{roll}}$ is the friction that the ground applies to the wheel and that the wheel applies to the aircraft axle (point A). Hence - now that the wheel is an independent body - the friction force is applied on the aircraft at the point A instead of the point C, so the code below is updated by the PR: https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/FGLGear.cpp#L725 Note that in this PR, $F_{\text{roll}}$ is used for 2 different purposes: 1. To apply the friction force to the aircraft body (as is currently the case) 2. To compute the driving torque $R\cdot F_{\text{roll}}$ (in blue on the picture above) that will be applied to the wheel. ### Braking management Unlike in the current code, the friction coefficient for $F_{\text{roll}}$ is always the static coefficient $\mu_{\text{static}}$ and is independent of the brake position `BrakePos`. To keep the braking feature, the patch introduces the braking torque $\tau_{brake}$ (in yellow on the picture above) that is currently not modeled by `FGLGear`. Hence the new Lagrange multiplier `ftWheelBrake` whose job is to zero out the relative motion between the wheel and the aircraft. The braking torque $\tau_{brake}$ obviously depends on the brake position `BrakePos` and is using `BrakeFCoeff`: https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/FGLGear.cpp#L590-L593 It is following that the wheel applies permanently a resisting torque $\mu_{\text{rolling}}F_{\text{roll}}R$ to the axle, whatever the braking position and this has 2 consequences: 1. The rolling friction coefficient is now characterizing the friction between the wheel and its axle. Legacy behavior is to assume that the rolling friction coefficient characterizes the hysteresis in the compression/expansion of the tire while rolling. There is nothing problematic in these two different interpretations of the rolling friction coefficient but model designers need to know that. 2. When the wheel is spinning $\tau_{\text{brake}}$ will **always** be equal to the maximum torque allowed by the Coulomb law i.e. $\tau_{\text{brake}}=\mu_{\text{brake}}F_{\text{roll}}R$ because the `ftWheelBrake` multiplier is targetting a *no wheel spin* condition. So, how is braking working, now? When applying some brake, $\tau_{brake}$ increases, $\omega$ decreases so $F_{\text{roll}}$ increases to try to restore the no slip condition $R\omega=v_A$. Note that $F_{\text{roll}}$ can reach $\mu_{\text{static}}F_n$ with the wheel still spinning. ### Wheel dynamics The driving torque and the braking torque are then used to compute the spin rate $\omega$ using the classic angular momentum equation $$I\dot{\omega}=R\cdot F_{\text{roll}}-\tau_{\text{brake}}$$ Note that there is a subtlety here: $\omega$ is the wheel spin rate **measured in the NED frame** (so-called *absolute spin rate* in the PR). This is deviating from what most people would expect i.e. a spin rate measured in the body frame: * This allows to define the no slip condition as $R\omega=V_{\text{axle}}$ instead of $R\omega=V_C$ where $V_C$ is the velocity at the contact point with respect to the ground (i.e. $V_C=V_G+\Omega_{\text{aircraft}}\times GC$). It simplifies the code a bit but; * The condition that the `ftWheelBrake` multiplier has to resolve is not $\omega=0$ but $$\omega=\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}\cdot\vec{u}_{\text{axle}}$$ ### No slip condition vs *no wheel spin* condition With respect to that point, the code in the PR is not so easy to understand because it is far from obvious that, for the `ftWheelBrake` multiplier, the following code actually simplifies to the equation above: ```c++ double wheelTerm = (mi->Wheel && dt > 0.) ? mi->WheelCoeff * mi->Wheel->Rate / dt : 0.; rhs[i] = -(DotProduct(U, vdot) + DotProduct(moment(mi), wdot) + wheelTerm)/d; ``` As a reminder, according to the following code: https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/FGAccelerations.cpp#L265-L273 we have (the terrain movement is ignored to simplify the analysis) $$\text{vdot}=\dfrac{d\vec{v}_G}{dt}+\dfrac{\vec{v}_G}{\Delta t}$$ $$\text{wdot}=\dfrac{d\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}}{dt}+\dfrac{\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}}{\Delta t}$$ So, for `ftWheelBrake`, we have $U=0$, `moment(mi)` is equal to $-u_{\text{axle}}$, `mi->WheelCoeff == 1.0`, and `mi->Wheel->Rate` is obviously $\omega$ so we have: $$\text{rhs}=\left(-\dfrac{d\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}}{dt}\cdot\vec{u}_{\text{axle}}+\dfrac{\omega-\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}\cdot\vec{u}_{\text{axle}}}{\Delta t}\right)\dfrac{1}{d}$$ where one can recognize the *no wheel spin* condition $\omega-\Omega_{\text{aircraft}}\cdot u_{\text{axle}}$ *Note: You can ignore the time derivation and the division by `d` because they are technical details unrelated to the point I am trying to make.* On the other hand, for the `ftRoll` multiplier, the same C++ code leads to the no slip condition because $U=u_{\text{roll}}$, `moment(mi)` is equal to $GA\times u_{\text{roll}}$ and `mi->Wheel->Rate` is equal to $-R$ so we have $$\text{rhs}=\left(\vec{u}_{\text{roll}}\cdot\left(\dfrac{d\vec{v}_G}{dt}+\dfrac{\vec{v}_G}{\Delta t}\right)+(\vec{GA}\times\vec{u}_{\text{roll}})\cdot\left(\dfrac{d\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}}{dt}+\dfrac{\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}}{\Delta t}\right)+\dfrac{-R\omega}{\Delta t}\right)\dfrac{1}{d}$$ which simplifies to (using the identity $(A\times B)\cdot C=(C\times A)\cdot B$) $$\text{rhs}=\left(\vec{u}_{\text{roll}}\cdot\left(\dfrac{d\vec{v}_G}{dt}+\dfrac{d\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}}{dt}\times\vec{GA}\right)-\dfrac{R\omega-\vec{u}_{\text{roll}}\cdot(\vec{v}_G+\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}\times\vec{GA})}{\Delta t}\right)\dfrac{1}{d}$$ and since the velocity at the axle is $v_A=v_G+{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}\times GA$, we finally have: $$\text{rhs}=\left(\vec{u}_{\text{roll}}\cdot\dfrac{d\vec{v}_A}{dt}-\dfrac{R\omega-\vec{u}_{\text{roll}}\cdot\vec{v}_A}{\Delta t}\right)\dfrac{1}{d}$$ where we recognize the no slip condition $R\omega-u_{\text{roll}}\cdot v_A$. So, great! the code works. However it has been a pain to understand that this code covers two entirely different conditions using some tricks: setting $U$ to 0 and the not-very-well-named `WheelCoeff` to either 1 or $-R$! ### Conclusion (for now) As claimed, the PR brings a better and more realistic handling of braking, wheel spin up energy, wheel spin up when touching ground, etc. However, the code deserves some clean up and there are a couple of errors that need to be addressed. To be continued... (sorry I'm running out of time for now but questions/comments on my analysis above are welcome).

Merci beaucoup @bcoconni for the addition of your writeup. In an ideal world every non-trivial bit of physics code in JSBSim would include a URL in the class/method pointing to writeups like this, i.e. markdown/jupyter style with snippets of explanatory text, equations, diagrams, snippets of code.

A few comments that should hopefully simplify and clarify the code.

After these have been implemented, the code should no longer need the lambda function `moment`, neither the members `LeverArm` or `UseMomentJacobian`.

After these have been discussed/implemented/rejected, I will have some other comments.
